title: Node.js Version Upgrades and Migration
learning_outcomes: Describe Supported version lines and explain how it relates to Node.js Version Upgrades and Migration.
Demonstrate Runtime compatibility in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Dependency verification.

content.intro: Node.js Version Upgrades and Migration is part of deployment and production operations. This lesson connects Supported version lines, Runtime compatibility, Dependency verification to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Database clients manage queries and connections; transactions and parameterized queries protect data integrity. Test concurrent updates, rollback behavior, connection failures, invalid input, and query plans as appropriate.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Database clients manage queries and connections; transactions and parameterized queries protect data integrity. Use parameterized SQL, a managed connection pool, bounded transactions, and reviewed schema migrations.

items.title: Supported version lines
items.text: For Supported version lines, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Runtime compatibility
items.text: For Runtime compatibility, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Dependency verification
items.text: For Dependency verification, identify the relevant Node.js API or runtime behavior, trace its inputs and observable result, then test one invalid input, failure, lifecycle edge, or version-dependent assumption. Avoid inferring correctness from a happy-path run alone.

items.title: Regression testing
items.text: Tests should assert observable behavior and include failure cases. Deterministic inputs and cleanup are more valuable than depending on network state or exact timing.

items.title: Staged production rollouts
items.text: Production readiness includes explicit configuration, health checks, observability, dependency management, and graceful shutdown; a local run alone does not verify deployment.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Node.js Version Upgrades and Migration. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Supported version lines; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Runtime compatibility, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Concatenating user input into SQL or holding transactions open while waiting for unrelated network work.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Bind values through the database driver and keep transaction boundaries short and explicit.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
